evidence: Ter. Heaut. 77: hūmānī nihil ā mē aliēnum putō
terms.comment: The human race is genus hūmānum (Cic. Amic. 20, Lewis & Short). Of a person, hūmānus also means “kind, civilised, cultivated” (hūmānitās).

terms.gloss: a mortal, a human (as against the gods)
terms.grammar: noun (the adjective mortālis used as a noun)
evidence: Verg. A. 1.327–328: haud tibi vultus mortālis

phrases.latin: Homō sum: hūmānī nihil ā mē aliēnum putō.
phrases.english: I am human: I count nothing human foreign to me.

phrases.latin: nūllās profectō terrās caelum contingere nec inexsuperābilēs hūmānō generī esse
phrases.english: no land actually touches the sky, and none is beyond the human race to cross

phrases.latin: maximum est elephāns proximumque hūmānīs sēnsibus
phrases.english: the largest is the elephant, and the nearest to human feeling

sources: Lewis & Short: humanus · Lewis & Short: homo · Lewis & Short: mortalis
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 330.

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-livius, loci-plinius, loci-vergilius), checked against the editions named there; Terence (Heaut. 77) checked against the Perseus Latin texts, where Parry prints nihil (the Oxford text nīl).
